messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 37
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Firefighter
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 62

# The Weight of Footsteps

Tariq is a 37-year-old Lebanese American firefighter who has spent the better part of a decade running toward danger for a living. He is the kind of man his crewmates describe as unflappable — the one who stays calm when a ceiling collapses, who cracks a dry joke while pulling hose through a burning hallway. His wife, Nadia, says he was always like that, steady as a wall. Neither of them could have predicted that what would finally break through that steadiness would not be fire or smoke, but a woman he barely knew.

It began about two years ago, quietly enough. A woman Tariq had briefly spoken with at a community fundraiser began appearing — at his fire station, outside his mosque, in the parking lot of the grocery store where Nadia shopped. At first Tariq dismissed it, embarrassed even to name what was happening. Men like him, he told himself, did not get rattled by someone standing on a sidewalk. But the notes came next, slipped under his windshield wipers. Then the phone calls to the station. Then photographs — of him, of Nadia, of their front door — mailed to their home with no return address. For eleven months, she was everywhere and nowhere, and the police, despite his reports, could do little until she crossed a threshold that always seemed just out of reach.

The stalking ended only after the woman was arrested for an unrelated offense and a restraining order was finally secured. By then, Tariq had already changed in ways that frightened him more than she ever had.

He cannot sleep past three in the morning. He wakes to the sound of nothing — a car passing, the house settling — and his body is already at full alert, heart hammering, sweat cooling on his chest. He lies in the dark and runs through the layout of his house, cataloguing the locks, calculating distances. Nadia has learned not to touch him when he wakes like that. Once she did, and the sound he made scared them both.

During the day, Tariq moves through the world with the hypervigilance of a man who has decided the world is a place where safety is always provisional. He scans parking lots before he gets out of his truck. He sits with his back to the wall in restaurants, something he used to laugh at other people for doing. He has quietly mapped three different routes between his home and the station and rotates them without telling anyone why.

At work, he functions. His training is so deeply embodied that he can still do the job, and he is grateful for that. But his crewmates have noticed he is shorter now, quicker to withdraw. He used to linger after shift, trading stories over bad coffee. Now he is in his truck before the bay doors are fully open. He tells himself it is because he wants to get home to Nadia, but the truth he does not say out loud is that he needs to check the house.

What haunts him most is not fear, exactly — it is shame. He has pulled people from burning buildings. He has held the hands of strangers in their worst moments. And yet the memory of finding that first photograph of Nadia on their doorstep can reduce him, without warning, to a man who cannot breathe in a grocery store. The intrusive images come sideways — her face in a crowd, a manila envelope on someone else's desk — and they carry with them a helplessness that feels unbearable to a man whose entire identity is built around being the one who helps.

He has not told Nadia the full extent of what is happening inside him. He worries it would frighten her. He worries, more quietly, that it would change the way she sees him. So he carries it the way he has always carried heavy things — alone, forward, without complaint, waiting for the weight to ease.
